comparisons.title: Desire vs. need
comparisons.contrast: Projected desire evaluates an imagined future identity or experience; practical need asks what absence would materially prevent. The categories may overlap but do not imply identical reasons for valuing an object.
comparisons.leftLens: What story or symbolic promise makes this appealing?
comparisons.rightLens: What essential function or obligation does this satisfy?
comparisons.illustration: Fictional: a collector wants a limited-edition coat while also needing a reliable jacket for winter. Either purchase can be reasonable, but the motivations should not be confused.
comparisons.ethics: Do not disguise a luxury aspiration as a necessity or shame someone for having symbolic preferences.

comparisons.title: Persuasion vs. coercion
comparisons.contrast: Autonomy-supportive persuasion invites reconsideration through reasons while preserving real refusal; coercion imposes penalties or threats that make compliance a poor indicator of agreement.
comparisons.leftLens: Can the person evaluate evidence and decline without undue penalty?
comparisons.rightLens: Is a credible threat, dependency or unacceptable cost compelling assent?
comparisons.illustration: Fictional: a team lead offers a voluntary scheduling pilot versus a lead threatening staff who refuse.
comparisons.ethics: Respect consent, disclose costs and avoid using deceptive reassurance as a substitute for genuine choice.

comparisons.title: Immediate rewards vs. decision horizon
comparisons.contrast: Immediate-reward salience describes which outcomes capture attention; decision horizon describes how far the evaluation extends. Close attention to today is not automatically a narrow or unsound decision.
comparisons.leftLens: Which vivid recent signals dominate attention?
comparisons.rightLens: Which delayed outcomes, alternatives and probabilities have been included?
comparisons.illustration: Fictional: an organization accepts a short-term subsidy after calculating its maintenance liabilities, rather than overlooking them because the offer is attractive.
comparisons.ethics: Avoid judging decisions solely by outcomes; assess information and available options at the time.

comparisons.title: Interpretive attitude vs. external circumstance
comparisons.contrast: Interpretive attitude concerns what a person anticipates and how they respond; external circumstance includes facts, resource constraints and others’ decisions that interpretation cannot simply remove.
comparisons.leftLens: What assumptions and reactions are changeable with new information?
comparisons.rightLens: What physical, social or institutional limitations remain regardless of expectation?
comparisons.illustration: Fictional: two job applicants can seek more feedback, yet an inaccessible transit route remains a real barrier for either one.
comparisons.ethics: Do not blame individuals for abuse, disability, discrimination, poverty or illness by reducing all outcomes to mindset.
